demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Triggers.value: Talk about people loosing loved ones

Threat.value: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
I feel on guard even inside my own home

Memory.value: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel like I don't know myself anymore
I feel isolated and set apart from others
My life has been destroyed by the trauma

issues.item: Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
issues.explanation: Physical pain in the same body parts as during the event is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma being an unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one, unless the patient was also physically injured during the event. That makes this item clinically implausible from the provided trauma context.

A global mistrust appraisal is a weak fit with bereavement trauma unless there is some interpersonal betrayal, negligence, or assault-related context. The rest of the profile centers on loss, alarm, and isolation rather than interpersonal threat from other people, so this item is not well supported by the trauma type or the other selected items.

For trauma involving the unexpected death of a loved one, ambulances can plausibly cue the death context and workplace cues may be idiosyncratically linked, but 'People cycling' is hard to connect clinically unless the loved one died in a cycling-related incident, which is not reflected anywhere else in threat, appraisals, or memory. It stands out as a trigger with no supporting context in the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Memory: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
issues.explanation: The memory profile is dominated by grief-related recall and affective reliving without clear imagery, which fits bereavement trauma. 'Intense shame' on recall is not impossible, but here it lacks support from the negative appraisals, which focus on identity loss, isolation, and life destruction rather than self-blame, guilt, or humiliation. In this profile, shame is insufficiently integrated with the rest of the formulation and trauma type.

vignette:
Samuel, a 55-year-old African American painter, found his world irrevocably altered on a Tuesday morning eight months ago. He had been on a scaffold, meticulously adding detail to a community mural, his 28-year-old son, Michael, working alongside him on a lower section. Suddenly, a terrible groaning sound ripped through the air, followed by a thunderous crash from an adjacent, unfinished wing of the building. Before Samuel could process what was happening, a heavy beam had given way, striking Michael. Samuel vividly remembered the sickening thud, the way Michael fell, and the immediate, frantic screams from others on site. His memories of that frightening event were mostly pictures: the dust cloud, the twisted metal, the desperate faces of the construction workers, and the specific, chilling yellow light of the ambulance as it finally arrived. He could still see the paramedics working over Michael, their grim expressions, and the moment they covered him.

In the weeks and months that followed, the world around Samuel began to morph into a landscape of constant reminders and threats. The sound of an ambulance siren, even from a distance, would instantly transport him back to that scene, the visual memories flashing before his eyes with overwhelming clarity. Sometimes, he would be hit by the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory at all, a sudden, crushing wave of despair and terror that left him gasping for air. His workplace, once a source of pride and creative solace, had become a minefield. The smell of paint, the height of a scaffold, the familiar hum of tools – all these things could trigger the vivid pictures and the profound grief that would wash over him. He found himself avoiding larger projects, turning down commissions that would take him to new construction sites, and even struggling to pick up a brush in his home studio.

What frightened Samuel most was the pervasive sense of danger that had taken root in his body and mind. He felt constantly tense, his muscles knotted, his nerves on edge, as if his body was perpetually ready to react to an unseen threat. This hyper-vigilance extended even to his own home, where he found himself on guard, listening intently to every creak and groan of the old house, unable to truly relax. As dusk fell, this feeling intensified; he found it harder to feel safe at night than during the day, the darkness amplifying his sense of vulnerability and making sleep a fractured, anxious experience. He would lie awake for hours, his heart pounding, convinced that something terrible was about to happen again.

The conversations that used to anchor him in his community now felt like traps. Any talk about people losing loved ones, whether a shared condolence or a story on the news, would send a cold dread through him, making him withdraw into himself. He had come to believe that his life had been utterly destroyed by the trauma, that the vibrant, passionate painter he once was had been extinguished. This feeling of profound loss extended to his very sense of self; he would often look in the mirror and feel like he didn't know the man staring back. He felt isolated and set apart from others, convinced that no one could truly understand the depth of his pain or the constant fear that now defined his existence. His wife, Maria, tried to reach him, but his withdrawal and constant edginess created a growing chasm between them. The financial strain from his inability to work consistently, coupled with his emotional distance, had become unbearable, pushing Samuel to finally seek help, not with hope, but with a desperate fear that he might lose what little he had left.
